newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Long contracts to stay as bedrock of EU gas market.
newsitem.headline: Long contracts to stay as bedrock of EU gas market.

text.p: Long-term take-or-pay (TOP) contracts will remain the cornerstone of gas trading in Europe despite liberalisation pressures and the development of spot and futures trading, European gas chiefs told the European Gas 97 conference on Tuesday.
But long term contracts, which provided hardship for British Gas, will likely follow the European model, involving regular re-negotiating of prices and volumes, or re-openers.

Mark Frevert, President and Chief Executive Officer of Enron Europe, had earlier said that long-term agreements were not necessary to finance production and downstream capital investments. Market-related products would emerge which would efficiently manage the risks, he said.

"To eliminate the basis for long term take or pay contracts in the futures will inevitably have a detrimental effect on the producers ability to execute new supply projects," said Peter Mellbye, executive vice president of Statoil A.S.
He added that, in Britain, where long-term contracts are "falling out of fashion", large price variations are likely.

"The price level determines when exploration and development are to be made...Since 1992, (reserves) have fallen from 24 years to 20 years. This of course reflects company behaviour in circumstances of increased uncertainty," he said.
Wilfried Czernie, senior general manager of Ruhrgas AG said such contracts are vital to ensure security of supply and to limit price fluctuations, particularly for large importers such as Germany.

"Long-term contracts with reliable planning parameters remain a must for all partners in order to make sure that there is no threat to the common goal of safeguarding the position of gas in Europe's energy supply," he said.
Germany, the largest European gas market, currently imports around 80 percent of its gas needs.
Paul Hallas, head of European commercial policy at newly formed Centrica also acknowledged that the British gas trading practices could not be entirely copied on the continent.

"Take-or-pay contracts with reopeners, as on the continent, are more flexible and robust. Short term and spot trades will grow in importance, but we're unlikely to see them supplanting existing TOP contracts," he said.

The vice president of Gaz de France said there was too much made of the similarities between the electricity and gas markets and not enough of the differences. Successful liberalising measures and short-term markets which might work in the former could not be applied to gas, he said.

He said discrepancies in reserves between member states, Europe's position as a net importer of gas were just two differences between the markets. But they were sufficient to make security of supply far more relevent in the gas industry, he said.

"It is possible to allow both long-term and short-term contracts, but the important points is that the directive should not only allow (them), but also allow for a market organisation which is compatible with the coexistence of these two types of contracts," he said.
